lec05kp23-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp23-u01-p1-title.text: A decision tree draws no complex boundary but asks one-feature yes/no questions, each cutting once

lec05kp23-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p1-bridge.text: The regression of KP22 fitted a line or curve. Can classification skip the boundary and ask a series of simple yes/no questions?

lec05kp23-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-partition
lec05kp23-u01-p1-fig1.text: Left: two axis-parallel questions cut the plane into regions A, B and C; right: the matching tree, each question testing one feature against a threshold.

image.alt: Left: two axis-parallel questions cut the plane into regions A, B and C; right: the matching tree, each question testing one feature against a threshold.

lec05kp23-u01-p1-term:決策樹.name: term:Decision tree
lec05kp23-u01-p1-term:決策樹.text: **Decision tree**: a series of yes/no decisions along a path of nodes, ruling out classes step by step until a leaf is reached.

lec05kp23-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p1-c1.text: **OBCT** (ordinary binary classification tree): every node asks one feature, '$x_i\le\alpha$?', cutting the space into hyper-rectangles parallel to the axes.

lec05kp23-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p1-c2.text: **Strengths**: especially good with many classes; often not every feature has to be tested; simple and easy to interpret; numeric and categorical features both work.

lec05kp23-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp23-u01-p2-title.text: Training fixes four things; thresholds are midpoints of neighbouring values, so 10 values give 9 candidates

lec05kp23-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p2-bridge.text: How is a tree grown? Every node asks one feature against a threshold, so what must each node decide, and how is a threshold chosen from infinitely many?

lec05kp23-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-cands
lec05kp23-u01-p2-fig1.text: The 10 distinct training values of one feature and the 9 midpoint thresholds between neighbours.

image.alt: The 10 distinct training values of one feature and the 9 midpoint thresholds between neighbours.

lec05kp23-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p2-c1.text: **Four things**: the set of candidate questions; the splitting criterion; the stop-splitting rule; the class-assignment rule for leaves.

lec05kp23-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p2-c2.text: **Candidates**: if $x_k$ has $N_{tk}$ distinct values in the node, take midpoints of neighbours as thresholds, at most $N_{tk}-1$ (the book writes $N_{tk}$); over all features the list is finite.

lec05kp23-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp23-u01-p3-title.text: Impurity is Shannon entropy: 1.522 for (4,4,2), 0 for one class, 1.585 at most for three

lec05kp23-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p3-bridge.text: Thresholds are midpoints of neighbouring values, giving 9 candidates. Which to pick? First measure how mixed the classes in a node are.

lec05kp23-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-entropy
lec05kp23-u01-p3-fig1.text: The two-class entropy curve peaks at probability 0.5; the impurity is 1.522 for (4,4,2), 1.585 for (1,1,1) and 0 for (5,0,0).

image.alt: The two-class entropy curve peaks at probability 0.5; the impurity is 1.522 for (4,4,2), 1.585 for (1,1,1) and 0 for (5,0,0).

lec05kp23-u01-p3-term:不純度.name: term:Impurity
lec05kp23-u01-p3-term:不純度.text: **Impurity** $I(t)=-\sum_iP(\omega_i|t)\log_2P(\omega_i|t)$: larger the more mixed the classes in the node.

lec05kp23-u01-p3-c1.name: u01-p3-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p3-c1.text: **Properties**: maximal when all classes are equal ($\log_2M$ for $M$ classes); 0 when all are of one class (with $0\log0=0$); probabilities are estimated by $N_t^i/N_t$.

lec05kp23-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp23-u01-p4-title.text: The impurity decrease ΔI: Example 4.2 recomputes from its own counts to 0.322, where the book prints 0.315

lec05kp23-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p4-bridge.text: Impurity is the Shannon entropy, 1.522 for (4,4,2). How much does a split lower it? Work through the book's Example 4.2 by hand.

lec05kp23-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-ex42
lec05kp23-u01-p4-fig1.text: Example 4.2: parent (4,4,2) with children (3,1,0) and (1,3,2); the recomputed ΔI is 0.322 where the book prints 0.315.

image.alt: Example 4.2: parent (4,4,2) with children (3,1,0) and (1,3,2); the recomputed ΔI is 0.322 where the book prints 0.315.

lec05kp23-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p4-c1.text: **Formula**: $\Delta I=I(t)-\tfrac{N_{tY}}{N_t}I(t_Y)-\tfrac{N_{tN}}{N_t}I(t_N)$; pick the question with the largest $\Delta I$.

lec05kp23-u01-p4-c3.name: u01-p4-c3
lec05kp23-u01-p4-c3.text: **Recomputed**: $\Delta I=1.522-0.4\cdot0.811-0.6\cdot1.459=0.322$; the book prints $I(t_Y)=0.815$, $I(t_N)=1.472$, $\Delta I=0.315$, which disagrees with its own counts (its printed numbers give only 0.312). Only this split was recomputed here.

lec05kp23-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp23-u01-p5-title.text: Children must be weighted by size: without it a split isolating one pure point looks best

lec05kp23-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p5-bridge.text: To pick the question with the largest ΔI, each child is multiplied by $N_{tY}/N_t$. What happens without it?

lec05kp23-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-weight
lec05kp23-u01-p5-fig1.text: Split A isolates one pure point and split B is balanced: weighted, B wins (0.278 against 0.108); unweighted, A wins (0.504 against 0.278).

image.alt: Split A isolates one pure point and split B is balanced: weighted, B wins (0.278 against 0.108); unweighted, A wins (0.504 against 0.278).

lec05kp23-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p5-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): a parent of 5 against 5 ($I=1$). Split A: Yes $(1,0)$, No $(4,5)$; split B: Yes $(4,1)$, No $(1,4)$.

lec05kp23-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p5-c2.text: **Weighted**: A $=0.108$, B $=0.278$, so B is chosen.

lec05kp23-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp23-u01-p5-c3.text: **Unweighted** (children simply averaged): A $=0.504$, B $=0.278$, so A is chosen; one pure point is mistaken for a big gain.

lec05kp23-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp23-u01-p6-title.text: As the tree grows from depth 1 to 12, training reaches 100% while new points stall near 85%

lec05kp23-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p6-bridge.text: Weighted ΔI keeps picking splits down the tree, even leaves with a single pure point appear. What happens when the tree is too large?

lec05kp23-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-depth
lec05kp23-u01-p6-fig1.text: Training and new-point accuracy of trees of depth 1 to 12 on two-moon data: training reaches 100% while new points stay near 85%.

image.alt: Training and new-point accuracy of trees of depth 1 to 12 on two-moon data: training reaches 100% while new points stay near 85%.

lec05kp23-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p6-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): two noisy half-moons (sd 0.35), 100 training and 1000 new points per class, entropy criterion.

lec05kp23-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp23-u01-p6-c3.text: **Meaning**: with more leaves training climbs to 100% while new points stay near 85%; a too-large tree learns the details of the training set.

lec05kp23-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp23-u01-p7-title.text: Grow then prune: cutting 24 leaves to 10 lifts new points from 85.1% to 87.3%

lec05kp23-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p7-bridge.text: With more leaves new points stay near 85%. The source says stopping on an impurity threshold stops too early or too late, so what to do?

lec05kp23-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-prune
lec05kp23-u01-p7-fig1.text: Pruning strengths 0, 0.01, 0.02 and 0.05 leave 24, 22, 10 and 7 leaves with 85.1%, 85.1%, 87.3% and 86.3% on new points.

image.alt: Pruning strengths 0, 0.01, 0.02 and 0.05 leave 24, 22, 10 and 7 leaves with 85.1%, 85.1%, 87.3% and 86.3% on new points.

lec05kp23-u01-p7-term:剪枝.name: term:Pruning
lec05kp23-u01-p7-term:剪枝.text: **Pruning**: grow a large tree first, then cut branches that are not worth their cost, judged by an error estimate plus complexity such as the leaf count.

lec05kp23-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p7-c1.text: **Results** (same data; α is the pruning strength): $\alpha=0$: 24 leaves, 100% training, 85.1% on new points; 0.01: 22 leaves, 85.1%; 0.02: 10 leaves, 96.5% / 87.3%; 0.05: 7 leaves, 94.0% / 86.3%.

lec05kp23-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p7-c2.text: **Honestly**: one dataset and one run, a gain of about 2 points. Entropy and Gini over 20 draws (depth 4) give 86.1±2.3% and 86.1±3.1% on new points: the criterion hardly matters (as the source says).

lec05kp23-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp23-u01-p8-title.text: Trees vary a lot; 25 bagged trees lift new points from 84.4% to 87.7%

lec05kp23-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p8-bridge.text: Pruning can cut branches that are not worth their cost, but the pruned tree is still one tree. How much does it change when the training set changes slightly, and can the variance be averaged out?

lec05kp23-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-bag
lec05kp23-u01-p8-fig1.text: New-point accuracy over 20 training sets: single tree 84.4±1.4, bagging 87.7±1.1, random forest 87.8±1.1; the root thresholds of 8 trees range from 0.09 to 0.42.

image.alt: New-point accuracy over 20 training sets: single tree 84.4±1.4, bagging 87.7±1.1, random forest 87.8±1.1; the root thresholds of 8 trees range from 0.09 to 0.42.

lec05kp23-u01-p8-term:Bagging.name: term:Bagging
lec05kp23-u01-p8-term:Bagging.text: **Bagging**: draw $B$ samples with replacement from the training set, grow a tree on each and take a majority vote.

lec05kp23-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p8-c1.text: **Variance** (designed here): on 8 training sets of the same size every first cut is on the second feature, with thresholds 0.42, 0.11, 0.12, 0.09, 0.22, 0.26, 0.22, 0.29 and 22 to 33 leaves.

lec05kp23-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p8-c2.text: **Averages** (20 training sets, new points): a single tree 84.4±1.4%; bagging with 25 trees 87.7±1.1%; a random forest (bagging plus random features per node) of 25 trees 87.8±1.1%.

lec05kp23-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp23-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: one oblique question is enough, an axis-parallel tree needs 13 to 14 leaves for about 95%

lec05kp23-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p9-bridge.text: Bagging averages out the variance, but the first cut is still parallel to an axis. What happens when the class boundary is oblique?

lec05kp23-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-oblique
lec05kp23-u01-p9-fig1.text: The class is set by the line x₁+x₂=0: axis-parallel trees of depth 1, 3 and 6 have 2, 7 and 13 leaves with 75.0%, 89.6% and 95.4% on new points.

image.alt: The class is set by the line x₁+x₂=0: axis-parallel trees of depth 1, 3 and 6 have 2, 7 and 13 leaves with 75.0%, 89.6% and 95.4% on new points.

lec05kp23-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p9-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): 300 points uniform on $[-1,1]^2$ with the class given by $x_1+x_2>0$; one oblique question $x_1+x_2\le0$ separates them exactly.

lec05kp23-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p9-c2.text: **Axis-parallel trees** (3000 new points): depth 1: 2 leaves, 75.0%; depth 3: 7, 89.6%; depth 6: 13, 95.4%; the full tree has 14 leaves, 100% training and 95.1% on new points.

lec05kp23-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp23-u01-p9-c3.text: **The price**: an oblique question $\sum c_kx_k\le\alpha$ cuts well but trains harder (source); fuzzy trees also exist.

lec05kp23-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp23-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, how much impurity each of two splits removes

lec05kp23-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p10-bridge.text: An axis-parallel tree picks each cut by $\Delta I$. By hand, how much impurity does each of two splits remove?

lec05kp23-u01-p10-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-practice
lec05kp23-u01-p10-fig1.text: Practice figure: a node of 4 against 4; split A gives (3,1) and (1,3), split B gives (2,2) and (2,2).

image.alt: Practice figure: a node of 4 against 4; split A gives (3,1) and (1,3), split B gives (2,2) and (2,2).

lec05kp23-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp23-u01-p10-q1.text: **Setup**: node $t$ has 4 points of $\omega_1$ and 4 of $\omega_2$; split A: Yes $(3,1)$, No $(1,3)$; split B: Yes $(2,2)$, No $(2,2)$. Given $I(3,1)=0.811$.

lec05kp23-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp23-u01-p10-q2.text: **Question 1**: what is $\Delta I$ of split A?

lec05kp23-u01-p10-q3.name: u01-p10-q3
lec05kp23-u01-p10-q3.text: **Question 2**: what is $\Delta I$ of split B, and which split is better?

lec05kp23-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp23-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2, A removes 0.189 and B removes 0

lec05kp23-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked what $\Delta I$ split A and split B give and how much impurity each removes. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp23-u01-p11-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-practice-sol
lec05kp23-u01-p11-fig1.text: Split A: ΔI=0.189; split B: ΔI=0, so A is better.

image.alt: Split A: ΔI=0.189; split B: ΔI=0, so A is better.

lec05kp23-u01-p11-a1.name: u01-p11-a1
lec05kp23-u01-p11-a1.text: **Question 1**: $I(t)=1$ (4 against 4); both children of A, $(3,1)$ and $(1,3)$, have $I=0.811$; $\Delta I=1-\tfrac48\cdot0.811-\tfrac48\cdot0.811=0.189$.

lec05kp23-u01-p11-a2.name: u01-p11-a2
lec05kp23-u01-p11-a2.text: **Question 2**: both children of B are $(2,2)$ with $I=1$; $\Delta I=1-0.5-0.5=0$.

lec05kp23-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp23-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: A is better; B removes no impurity at all, a wasted cut. A split into $(4,0)$ and $(0,4)$ would give $\Delta I=1$.

steps.label: Decision trees
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. The OBCT, the four design ingredients, the candidate questions, the entropy impurity and impurity decrease, stopping and class assignment, pruning, the high variance, bagging and random forests, oblique questions and the 'to remember' line follow the source; every number was recomputed by a program and these experiments were designed for this lecture (added). In particular the book's Example 4.2 prints I(tN)=1.472 and delta I=0.315, which recompute from its own counts to 1.459 and 0.322, and the pages say so. They also state honestly that a too-large tree stays near 85% on new points, that pruning gains only 2 points in one run and that the choice between entropy and Gini hardly matters. Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: A series of yes/no questions
steps.speakerNotes: The regression of KP22 fitted a line or curve. This page asks whether classification can skip the boundary and ask a series of simple yes/no questions. First the decision tree: a series of yes/no decisions along a path of nodes, ruling out classes step by step until a leaf is reached. The most popular is the OBCT: every node asks one feature, is x_i at most alpha, cutting the space into hyper-rectangles parallel to the axes. Strengths: especially good with many classes; often not every feature has to be tested; simple and easy to interpret; numeric and categorical features both work. The figure shows three regions on the left and the matching tree on the right. The next page asks how the tree is grown.

steps.label: Four ingredients
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said every node of a decision tree asks one feature. This page asks how a tree is grown, what each node must decide and how a threshold is chosen from infinitely many. Training fixes four things: the set of candidate questions; the splitting criterion; the stop-splitting rule; and the class-assignment rule for leaves. Candidates: if feature x_k has N_tk distinct values in the node, take midpoints of neighbouring values as thresholds, at most N_tk minus 1, whereas the book writes N_tk; over all features the list is finite. The example was designed here: 10 distinct values give 9 midpoints. The next page asks which of the 9 candidate questions to pick.

steps.label: Impurity
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page listed the splitting criterion among the four things. This page asks which of the 9 candidate questions to pick, which first requires measuring how mixed the classes in a node are. Impurity is the Shannon entropy: minus the sum of each class probability times its base-2 logarithm; larger the more mixed the classes in the node. Properties: maximal when all classes are equal, log2 M for M classes; 0 when all are of one class, with 0 times log 0 defined as 0; probabilities are estimated by N_t^i over N_t. Examples: (4, 4, 2) gives 1.522, where the book writes 1.521; (1, 1, 1) gives log2 3, which is 1.585; (5, 0, 0) gives 0. The left of the figure is the entropy curve for two classes, maximal at probability 0.5. The next page uses impurity to judge a split.

steps.label: Impurity decrease
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page defined impurity. This page asks how much a split lowers it, working through the book's Example 4.2 by hand. The formula: delta I is the impurity of the parent minus N_tY over N_t times the impurity of the Yes child minus N_tN over N_t times that of the No child; pick the question with the largest delta I. Example 4.2: t is (4, 4, 2), Yes is (3, 1, 0), No is (1, 3, 2): I of t is 1.522, I of t_Y is 0.811 and I of t_N is 1.459. Recomputed: delta I is 1.522 minus 0.4 times 0.811 minus 0.6 times 1.459, which is 0.322; the book prints 0.815, 1.472 and 0.315, which disagree with its own counts. Only this split was recomputed here. The next page asks why the children are weighted.

steps.label: Why weighting
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the impurity of each child in delta I is multiplied by N_tY over N_t. This page asks what happens without it. The setup was designed here: a parent of 5 against 5 with impurity 1. Split A: Yes is (1, 0) and No is (4, 5); split B: Yes is (4, 1) and No is (1, 4). Weighted: A is 0.108 and B is 0.278, so B is chosen. Unweighted, with the two children simply averaged: A is 0.504 and B is 0.278, so A is chosen; one pure point is mistaken for a big gain. The next page asks how large the tree should grow.

steps.label: How large a tree
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said weighted delta I keeps picking splits down the tree, even leaves with a single pure point appear. This page asks what happens when the tree is too large. The setup was designed here: two noisy half-moons with standard deviation 0.35, 100 training and 1000 new points per class, entropy criterion. Results, training and new points: depth 1 with 2 leaves gives 76.5% and 73.3%; depth 2 with 4 leaves gives 89.0% and 83.7%; depth 4 with 11 leaves gives 90.0% and 82.2%; depth 8 with 20 leaves gives 99.0% and 85.2%; depth 12 with 24 leaves gives 100% and 85.1%. The meaning is that with more leaves training climbs to 100% while new points stay near 85%; a too-large tree learns the details of the training set. The next page asks what to do.

steps.label: Pruning
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said new points stay near 85% with more leaves. This page asks what to do, since the source says stopping on an impurity threshold stops too early or too late. First pruning: grow a large tree first, then cut branches that are not worth their cost, judged by an error estimate plus complexity such as the leaf count. Results on the same data, alpha being the pruning strength: alpha 0 gives 24 leaves, 100% training and 85.1% on new points; 0.01 gives 22 leaves and 85.1%; 0.02 gives 10 leaves with 96.5% and 87.3%; 0.05 gives 7 leaves with 94.0% and 86.3%. Honestly: one dataset and one run, a gain of about 2 points. Entropy and Gini over 20 draws at depth 4 give 86.1 plus or minus 2.3 and 86.1 plus or minus 3.1 on new points, so the criterion hardly matters, as the source says. The next page asks how much the tree changes when the training set changes slightly.

steps.label: Variance and bagging
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said a pruned tree is still one tree. This page asks how much the tree changes when the training set changes slightly and whether the variance can be averaged out. First bagging: draw B samples with replacement from the training set, grow a tree on each and take a majority vote. The variance experiment was designed here: on 8 training sets of the same size every first cut is on the second feature, with thresholds 0.42, 0.11, 0.12, 0.09, 0.22, 0.26, 0.22 and 0.29, and 22 to 33 leaves. Averages over 20 training sets on new points: a single tree 84.4 plus or minus 1.4; bagging with 25 trees 87.7 plus or minus 1.1; a random forest of 25 trees 87.8 plus or minus 1.1. Why: a tree is hierarchical, so an error high up reaches every leaf below; averaging lowers the variance. A random forest picks one random feature per node, which hardly helped further here. The next extension page looks at oblique questions.

steps.label: Extension: oblique questions
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said bagging averages out the variance but the first cut is still parallel to an axis. This extension asks what happens when the class boundary is oblique. The setup was designed here: 300 points uniform on the square from minus 1 to 1, with the class given by x1 plus x2 above 0; one oblique question, x1 plus x2 at most 0, separates them exactly. Axis-parallel trees on 3000 new points: depth 1 has 2 leaves and 75.0%; depth 3 has 7 and 89.6%; depth 6 has 13 and 95.4%; the full tree has 14 leaves, 100% training and 95.1% on new points. The price: an oblique question cuts well but trains harder, as the source says; fuzzy trees also exist. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said an axis-parallel tree picks each cut by delta I. This page poses an exercise: by hand, how much impurity does each of two splits remove? Node t has 4 points of omega 1 and 4 of omega 2; split A: Yes is (3, 1) and No is (1, 3); split B: Yes is (2, 2) and No is (2, 2); given I of (3, 1) equal to 0.811. Question 1: what is delta I of split A? Question 2: what is delta I of split B, and which split is better? Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: I of t is 1, for 4 against 4; both children of A, (3, 1) and (1, 3), have impurity 0.811; delta I is 1 minus four eighths times 0.811 minus four eighths times 0.811, which is 0.189. Question 2: both children of B are (2, 2) with impurity 1; delta I is 1 minus 0.5 minus 0.5, which is 0. Check: A is better; B removes no impurity at all, a wasted cut; a split into (4, 0) and (0, 4) would give delta I equal to 1. That finishes decision trees; the next knowledge point looks at combining classifiers.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP23: decision trees, OBCT, splitting criteria and pruning (undergraduate, self-study)
